title: Improving Visual Token Reduction via Rectifying Distortions for Efficient Multimodal LLM Inference
claim: Reindexing or retaining positions after token reduction distorts position or attention; rectifying both restores a faithful representation.
layout: 2x2 panels (a)-(d) with shared legend below; smiley/frown status indicators
description: A 2x2 grid of token-sequence diagrams, each a row of small squares (gray system, light-blue visual, peach text tokens) with curved black arrows from the last token back to earlier ones, showing attention and positional bias. Below each row is a bracketed sys/vis/txt bar. Panel (a) shows the full sequence. Panel (b) reindexes positions, leaving a dashed empty region. Panel (c) keeps original indices with dashed placeholder squares for dropped tokens, and the text tokens turn orange. Panel (d), the proposed fix, adds blue plus signs under tokens and darker blue retained visual tokens. Green or red 'Position' and 'Attention' labels with smiley, neutral or frowning faces give the verdict for each panel. A boxed legend at the bottom explains the token colors and arrow types.
caption: Illustration of the impact of visual token reduction on the internal attention mechanism of the LLM within MLLMs (e.g., LLaVA [ref]). (a) The full token sequence. (b) Reindexing position indices assigns contiguous indices to the reduced sequence. (c) Retaining position indices preserves the original indices of the retained tokens from (a). (d) We rectify distortions by retaining original position indices and calibrating the attention weights of the retained tokens.
abstract: Recent advancements in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have achieved remarkable success in vision-language tasks, yet the quadratic computational complexity arising from the vast number of visual tokens incurs significant memory and latency bottlenecks. While visual token reduction (VTR) strategies have been explored to mitigate this burden, existing methods overlook the positional and attentional consistency between the full and reduced sequences, resulting in a distorted representation. To this end, we propose RESTORE, a novel VTR framework that rectifies the positional and attentional distortions while maintaining efficiency. Specifically, we present a simple yet effective calibration method that restores lost visual attention by augmenting attention weights based on relative distances. We also introduce a distinctive anchor selection for token merging to mitigate information loss during feature averaging. Experimental results on multiple benchmarks demonstrate that our method consistently improves the accuracy of various reduction methods, achieving state-of-the-art performance while maintaining computational efficiency. Project page is available at https://cvlab.yonsei.ac.kr/projects/RESTORE
